The modes

A frame is one JTTY frame, one FT8/FT4 transmission, one RTTY character, or one PSK31 character of average length for lower-case text. Gross bit rate counts every channel bit while transmitting (sync, FEC, start/stop, Varicode gaps); net bit rate counts information bits. The measured bandwidth holds 99% of the power of each mode's actual rendered signal.

Channel

This run used MM Watterson fading (Mid latitude, moderate (CCIR 'moderate')): two equal-strength Rayleigh-fading paths with a Gaussian Doppler spread of 0.5 Hz, the second delayed 1 ms. As in WSJT-X's own simulators, each transmission is renormalized to its clean power, so the SNR is the average over the transmission. Band noise is added after the fading.

Choosing a fading model: a station on Long Island, NY

Long Island (about 40.8° N, 73° W) sits near 50° N geomagnetic latitude, because the geomagnetic pole (about 81° N) lies at almost the same longitude. That makes it a mid-latitude station, but fading depends on the whole propagation path:

  • MM (mid-latitude moderate) — the primary model: domestic paths and most transatlantic contest contacts, i.e. most ARRL RTTY Roundup traffic.
  • MQ and MD — bracket it: a quiet day and an unsettled or multihop day.
  • HM (high-latitude moderate) — the stress case: northern transatlantic paths to Scandinavia and NE Europe pass near Labrador and Greenland (about 60–65° geomagnetic, the auroral oval's edge), polar paths to Japan and Asia cross it, and in geomagnetic storms (Kp ≥ 6–7) the oval reaches about 50°, so even nearby paths flutter.
  • LM (low-latitude moderate) — optional, for paths to South America and Africa across the geomagnetic equator; LD only for night-time equatorial spread-F.

Run the recommended set with one run per channel: for ch in MQ MM MD HM; do ./run_study.sh --channel $ch --run-name li-$ch; done

5-character decode rate

The headline curve: the share of transmitted 5-character groups printed exactly, for every mode. Five characters is a callsign's worth (W9XYZ), the shortest piece of text that is useful on its own, so a group counts only when all its characters print as one unbroken piece; garbage between groups does not break them. Each message is cut into groups from its start, and a final 1–4 characters form a short group of their own. An FT8 or FT4 message gives all its groups or none. The diamonds mark each mode's 80% point; the legend gives its value.

Contest QSO: time and bits to complete an exchange

The S&P station (W9XYZ in WI) answers K1ABC (in MA) running, from the S&P's call to the final TU/RR73. As overs, JTTY sends its native function-key atoms (a call is one frame, an exchange one frame), and RTTY and PSK31 send the same text in capitals. As macros, JTTY, PSK31 and RTTY send a typical contest macro with the exchange sent twice: JTTY as plain text, PSK31 and RTTY with CR/LF framing. PSK31's airtime includes fldigi's 1 s preamble and postamble on every over. FT8 and FT4 have no macros, so they appear on both graphs; they use their RU contest mode for RTTY Roundup and the standard QSO for the serial contest, one T/R slot per over. Best case is the error-free time (airtime only, no turnaround). Median is the median time of simulated QSOs, using the measured copy probability of each over at each SNR (an over or macro with an ambiguous field counts as not copied; see Contest exchanges): JTTY, RTTY and PSK31 repeat a failed over after an AGN? request, which may itself need repeating; FT8 and FT4 lose a whole T/R cycle per failed over.

Overs

Macros

Contest exchanges copied exactly

Overs

Each over of the reference QSOs printed with no error, and with no information field (a call or an exchange) also printed with a conflicting value elsewhere in the printout. FT8 and FT4 appear on both graphs with their QSO messages; their decodes are whole, CRC-checked messages, so the ambiguity rule does not apply to them.

Macros

A macro counts as copied when every required word (the call, the exchange, an AGN? request) prints exactly in at least one of its repetitions and no call or exchange is ambiguous. A field is ambiguous when the same information is received with a different value, so the operator cannot tell which is right: a printed word that could pass for the field (the same length, at most 2 characters different, or 1 for fields of 3 characters or fewer such as a state) without being any sent word. W4LEW W4LEW printed as QRLEW W4LEW is not copied; printed as W4LEW with the other copy lost, it is. A fragment such as 2BMJ for KE2BMJ, a word of another length, or junk with any symbol other than a trailing query mark (HA<JDU, K2AB?D, since every call, state and serial is letters and digits) does not make a field ambiguous. A ? at the end of a word is read as a query and ignored, so K2ABD? reads as K2ABD.

JTTY copy by message length

A JTTY message is copied exactly only if every frame and its end-of-message flag decode, so longer messages need more signal.

Character error rate of free text

RTTY-style print quality on keyboard-to-keyboard sentences: edit distance between what was sent and what printed, divided by the sent length, shown up to 50% because copy above that is likely unreadable. Dashed: noncoherent-FSK theory for RTTY with ideal character sync. Dotted: ideal differential-BPSK theory for PSK31 (a character lost if any of its bits is).

Throughput

Correctly copied text per minute of airtime, folding each mode's speed and its errors into one operator-facing number. At each SNR it is 60 × (characters copied, summed over every trial at that SNR) ÷ (seconds of airtime, summed over the same trials). Characters are those of the sent message after normalizing it: upper case, each run of spaces read as one space, none at the ends. Spaces between words count (except at JTTY frame boundaries, below); framing does not.

  • Characters copied. RTTY and PSK31: the characters of the message's 5-character groups that printed whole (the headline unit), so scattered characters matched by chance in noise count nothing. JTTY: the text of each frame the decoder printed correctly, with the spaces at the frame's two ends left out, whether or not the rest of the message arrived; a space between two words that falls at a frame boundary is therefore not counted, so a fully copied JTTY message counts fewer characters than its normalized text (about 7% fewer for free text, 2% for contest overs) (JTTY contest macros count every character of the macro's words). FT8 and FT4: every character of the message when it decoded, none when it did not. Contest macros (JTTY, RTTY and PSK31): every character of the macro's words when the macro counts as copied (the call and one copy of the exchange), none when it does not.
  • Airtime. RTTY: the whole transmission at 45.45 baud with 1.5 stop bits – 0.1 s of steady mark, two LTRS idle characters, the framing spaces, the message with its shift characters, and two LTRS at the end. PSK31: the whole transmission at 31.25 baud – 32 bits of preamble, the framing spaces, the message in Varicode (free text is sent in lower case, whose Varicode is shorter; contest overs in capitals), 32 bits of postamble, and one symbol each of envelope rise and fall. JTTY: the rendered transmission, a whole number of 1.888 s frames. FT8 and FT4: one whole 15 s / 7.5 s T/R slot per message, since each message takes a slot. A contest macro's airtime is its whole transmission, the repeated exchange (and the RTTY and PSK31 CR/LF) included.

Contest overs

FT8 and FT4 appear here with their QSO messages, the same series as the contest-overs copy chart.

Contest macros

The same overs as typical contest macros with the exchange sent twice (JTTY sends the same words, without CR/LF). A macro counts as copied when the call and one copy of the exchange print exactly. FT8 and FT4 have no macros, so their QSO messages are repeated here for reference.

Ragchew text

Free-text sentences. FT8 and FT4 have no free-text series in this study.

Reported vs true SNR

What each decoder prints as the signal report against the true SNR. Reports cannot go below a decoder's floor (JTTY −21 dB, FT4 −21 dB, FT8 −25 dB); where they hit it, the mean comes from a censored-normal fit rather than dropping them.

Strong-signal failures

Trials at least 3 dB above each series' 90% decode point that were still not a clean copy. Split: JTTY decoded every frame but printed the message over several lines. No EOM: every frame in one line but no end-of-message. Ambiguous: a contest field printed right but also with a conflicting value. False text: wrong text printed alongside.

Thresholds

SNR is true SNR at the antenna in a 2500 Hz reference bandwidth. The 80% point is read from the measured decode curve, fitted to never fall as SNR rises, with bootstrap intervals; a dash means it was not reached by +10 dB. Reported is what the decoder printed on average near the 80% point (a censored-normal fit where reports hit the decoder's floor).

Eb/N0 = SNR + 10·log10(2500 Hz / net bit rate), with JTTY 34 information bits per 1.888 s frame, FT8 and FT4 77 bits per 12.64 s / 5.04 s transmission, RTTY only the 5 data bits of each 7.5-bit character (start, stop and shift characters are overhead), and PSK31 5 bits per character at the mean Varicode length of the text each series sent (lower-case free text is shorter than contest capitals). Trials are transmissions; units are what decode % counts: 5-character groups, except one per whole contest macro. Intervals come from a bootstrap over whole trials, so groups sharing a transmission are not treated as independent.

Method

  • Every trial is generated, put through a simulated HF station, and decoded: JTTY, FT8 and FT4 are rendered and decoded by this WSJT-X tree's own wsjt-codec (JTTY through the GUI's receive path); RTTY and PSK31 by C reference modulators and matched-filter demodulators.
  • Channel: MM Watterson fading plus AWGN. SNR is the WSJT-X convention: signal power over noise power in 2500 Hz, at the antenna.
  • Receiver: USB with a 300–2700 Hz SSB filter for JTTY/FT8/FT4/PSK31; RTTY through a 1960–2460 Hz filter. AGC off; no-signal level 30 dB on the WSJT-X meter; 16-bit audio at 12 kHz.
  • JTTY: Rx 1500 Hz, F Tol 20 Hz (GUI defaults), transmitter within ±10 Hz, random start time. Lowest SNR report −21 dB.
  • FT8/FT4: Deep decoding with a-priori (AP) decoding off; decoders search the rig's 300–2700 Hz passband; random frequency across the passband and DT within about ±0.5 s.
  • RTTY: 45.45 baud, 170 Hz shift (mark 2125 / space 2295 Hz), 1.5 stop bits, US-TTY Baudot with unshift-on-space; tuning error up to ±5 Hz, no AFC. Only characters printed while the message was on the air are scored.
  • PSK31: BPSK31 at 31.25 baud, G3PLX Varicode, carrier 1000 Hz (fldigi default), 32 preamble reversals and 32 bits of postamble carrier. The operator's click lands up to ±5 Hz off; the decoder snaps to the signal within ±10 Hz as fldigi does, then tracks it with AFC. Differential detection after a matched filter; no squelch. Free text in lower case, contest overs in capitals.
  • Messages: reference contest QSO overs (RTTY Roundup and serial-number) and ragchew sentences for JTTY, RTTY and PSK31 (the same texts at the same trial; PSK31 types the sentences in lower case), and the equivalent FT8/FT4 QSO messages.
  • SNR grid: a pilot sweep from −21 to +10 dB in 1 dB steps (100 trials per point), extended downward 1 dB at a time until each curve is at or below 1%; then a 0.5 dB grid at full trials over each curve's 1–99% span plus 3.0 dB each side, up to at most +10 dB. Charts show both, from −21 to +10 dB.
  • Run: seed 2027, 1000 trials per fine-grid point (100 at pilot points), wsjtx-3.3.0-beta5, wsjt-codec SHA-256 4327849cb9c5db3c….

Caveats

  • AWGN is the standard benchmark, not the whole of HF: fading, QRN impulses and QRM change the picture (see the Channel section for fading runs).
  • JTTY searches its Rx frequency ± F Tol plus fixed channels over 1200–1800 Hz (about 600 Hz) and has no common time reference; FT8/FT4 search the whole 2.4 kHz passband but know when each period starts. A narrower search has fewer false starts, which can be worth a fraction of a dB.
  • The RTTY decoder is a careful reference implementation (about 1 dB from ideal noncoherent FSK), not MMTTY or 2Tone.
  • The PSK31 decoder is likewise a reference implementation (differential detection about 1 dB from ideal DBPSK near 1% bit errors, from the matched filter's inter-symbol interference), not fldigi.
  • Every mode is scored in 5-character groups, but they are lost differently: an FT8 or FT4 message decodes whole or not at all and a JTTY frame nearly so, while RTTY and PSK31 lose characters one at a time, so one lost character costs its group. A message's final short group (1-4 characters) can be matched by chance in garbage printed from noise. Compare thresholds with the Eb/N0 column, and contest throughput with the contest-QSO section.
  • Runs with the same seed share their trials, so two runs agreeing is not independent confirmation; replicate with a different --seed.
  • At strong signals JTTY split 51 of 49400 messages over two lines and printed false text in 104; see Strong-signal failures.
